This initial mass is considerably smaller than the adult female's ultimate size, suggesting a substantial period of intensive parental provisioning lies ahead. The fledgling, though capable of short flights, remains dependent on its parents for several weeks thereafter, gradually refining its foraging skills. This period of post-fledging care is essential for learning to identify and process the seeds of saltmarsh plants and coastal shrub berries, which form the bulk of the species' diet, before the young bird must achieve nutritional independence.

However, despite achieving physiological readiness early, many individuals may delay actual breeding until they have secured a territory and a mate, a process that can extend the pre-breeding period.
